item.title: Prosecutors ask for 25 years for man who sold products used by 93 to kill themselves
item.description:
Prosecutors ask for 25 years for man who sold products used by 93 to kill themselves
Prosecutors sought a 25-year prison sentence for a Canadian man who sold products online knowing buyers were likely to use them to kill themselvesByThe Associated PressNovember 27, 2026, 4:13 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
NEWMARKET, Ontario -- Ontario prosecutors on Friday sought a 25-year prison sentence for a Canadian man who pleaded guilty to aiding 14 suicides after selling products online knowing buyers were likely to use them to kill themselves.
Kenneth Law, 61, apologized to victims’ families from the prisoner’s box, saying that his actions were “categorically wrong” and promising never to repeat them.
Prosecutors argued that Law was motivated by money. His lawyers sought a 12-year sentence, describing him as a misguided believer in the right to die rather than a “mercenary predator.” A sentencing decision is expected in February.
Law pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of counseling or aiding suicide involving people in Ontario. The judge is also considering the deaths of 79 people in the United Kingdom.
At a hearing in September, families of people who died after buying lethal products from Law described their lives shattered by grief. Police said Law sold sodium nitrite, a substance commonly used to cure meats that can be deadly if ingested.
___
EDITOR’S NOTE — This story includes discussion of suicide. The U.S. suicide and crisis lifeline is available by calling or texting 988. There is also an online chat at 988lifeline.org. In the U.K., the Samaritans can be reached at 116 123 or www.samaritans.org.
___
Prosecutor Katie Doherty said 93 people, including 12 teenagers, died after using Law’s products.

item.title: UN rapporteur Albanese in limbo at airport after being denied entry to Costa Rica
item.description:
UN rapporteur Albanese in limbo at airport after being denied entry to Costa Rica
Francesca Albanese, the U.N. special rapporteur on human rights in the occupied Palestinian territories, is stranded at Costa Rica’s main airport awaiting for a court to decide whether she could enter the country after immigration authorities blocked h...ByJAVIER CÓRDOBA Associated PressNovember 27, 2026, 1:38 PM
SAN JOSÉ, Costa Rica -- Francesca Albanese, the U.N. special rapporteur on human rights in the Palestinian territories, was stranded in an airport terminal on Friday after being denied entry to Costa Rica.
Albanese posted a photo on X showing a suitcase beside a row of empty seats, with the caption: “This is where I will spend my first night in Costa Rica.”
She is awaiting a court decision on whether she can enter the country or must leave.
Costa Rican immigration authorities blocked her entry on Thursday, saying she was the subject of an international “alert” over alleged ties to terrorism and that her presence posed a national security risk.
Albanese is a high-profile independent investigator scrutinizing human rights abuses in the Palestinian territories. She is among a group of experts appointed by the 47-member U.N. Human Rights Council in Geneva to monitor and report on human rights conditions in individual countries and the observance of specific rights worldwide.
She was sanctioned by the United States in July 2025 over her work and sharp criticism of U.S. and Israeli policies during the war in Gaza. Secretary of State Marco Rubio described her actions as a “campaign of political and economic warfare against the United States and Israel.”
Albanese had traveled to Costa Rica at the invitation of the University of Costa Rica, which was scheduled to award her an honorary doctorate.

item.title: Mexico files formal complaint to US over DEA tip line
item.description:
Mexico files formal complaint to US over DEA tip line
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum says the country is filing a formal complaint with the U.S. over a Drug Enforcement Agency tip line for anonymous reports about criminals and corrupt Mexican officialsByFABIOLA SÁNCHEZ Associated PressNovember 27, 2026, 1:22 PM
Share
MEXICO CITY -- MEXICO CITY (AP) — Mexico filed a formal complaint with the U.S. over a Drug Enforcement Agency tip line for anonymous reports about criminals and corrupt Mexican officials, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said Friday, escalating a fight over a move she called interference in its internal affairs.
“We have made it very clear in our relationship with the United States that the relationship is one of coordination, not subordination,” she said in her daily news briefing.
The protest comes as U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration is pressuring Mexico to intensify its fight against cartels. It's made a public offer to deploy troops on Mexican soil, something Sheinbaum has ruled out.
DEA chief Terry Cole announced on his X account Wednesday that the agency was opening an anonymous tip line to receive information about members and associates of designated terrorist organizations, corrupt officials who support them, criminal networks and people who launder money to finance narcoterrorism in Sinaloa.
The northern state is the stronghold of one of Mexico's most powerful cartels, the Sinaloa Cartel, which Washington designated a terrorist organization along with five other Mexican criminal groups. Cole said the agency also plans to open a tip line for the state of Jalisco.
Sheinbaum once again urged Washington to address drug use and combat drug traffickers within its own territory. She also reaffirmed that Mexico would continue working to confront cartels and prevent drugs from reaching the U.S.

item.title: Canada’s Supreme Court largely upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
item.description:
Canada’s Supreme Court largely upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
Canada’s Supreme Court upheld most of a Quebec law banning schoolteachers, police officers and other public employees in positions of authority from wearing religious symbols at work, affirming the province’s use of a constitutional power to override c...ByThe Associated PressNovember 27, 2026, 10:59 AM
Share
OTTAWA, Ontario -- Canada’s Supreme Court on Friday upheld most of a Quebec law banning public schoolteachers, police officers and other public employees in positions of authority from wearing religious symbols at work, affirming the province’s constitutional power to override certain rights.
The 2019 law, known as Bill 21, prohibits religious symbols including Muslim headscarves, Sikh turbans, Jewish skullcaps and Christian crosses for workers covered by the ban.
The court upheld Quebec’s use of the “notwithstanding clause,” which allows lawmakers to override certain protections in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, Canada’s equivalent of the U.S. Bill of Rights. Those include religious freedom and equality rights. Lawmakers must renew the override every five years to keep it in effect.
The justices affirmed that lawmakers can invoke the clause before courts determine whether a law violates those rights.
The court upheld a finding that members of Quebec’s legislature cannot be required to perform their duties with their faces uncovered.
Quebec says the law ensures the separation of religion and government. Opponents say it discriminates against religious minorities, particularly Muslim women wearing headscarves.
“In the 21st century, entire categories of people are now barred from entire sectors of employment, not because of what they have done, but because of who they are,” said Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims.

item.title: Lula’s choice of Bradesco banker as Brazil’s finance minister lifts markets
item.description:
Lula’s choice of Bradesco banker as Brazil’s finance minister lifts markets
Brazilian markets have rallied after President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva confirmed that veteran banker Luiz Carlos Trabuco would lead his finance ministry in 2027, a move seen as a commitment to fiscal disciplineByELÉONORE HUGHES Associated PressNovember 27, 2026, 10:15 AM
RIO DE JANEIRO -- Brazilian markets rallied on Friday after President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva confirmed that he had chosen a veteran banker to lead the finance ministry in 2027, a move seen as a sign of his commitment to fiscal discipline.
Brazil’s currency, the real, and its stock market had tumbled after Lula’s surprise victory over Flávio Bolsonaro in last month’s presidential election. Investors had been counting on a win by Bolsonaro, who had pledged to slash spending.
But the announcement late Thursday that Bradesco chief Luiz Carlos Trabuco had accepted Lula’s invitation to oversee the country’s finances during his upcoming fourth term, which begins Jan. 5, triggered a sharp rebound.
The real strengthened from 5.88 to the dollar on Wednesday to 5.53 on Friday morning, while stocks surged between Thursday evening and Friday morning.
The currency had already begun strengthening after Brazil’s lower house approved a government plan earlier this week to control spending and increase revenue. Although many investors considered the plan too timid, they viewed it as a step in the right direction.
The package has drawn criticism from some of Lula’s supporters, who accuse his government of bowing to market pressure. They see the measures as a threat to health, education and welfare spending, as well as to his campaign promises.

item.title: Death toll in Pakistan building collapse rises to 8 with about 10 missing
item.description:
Death toll in Pakistan building collapse rises to 8 with about 10 missing
The death toll from the collapse of a six-story building under construction in southern Pakistan has risen to eightByThe Associated PressNovember 27, 2026, 8:48 AM
KARACHI, Pakistan -- The death toll from the collapse of a six-story building under construction in southern Pakistan rose to eight Friday after rescuers recovered four more bodies, officials said.
Rescuers are still searching for about 10 people believed trapped beneath the rubble of the building, which collapsed Wednesday in Karachi’s Baloch Colony neighborhood, police official Raja Sarwar said.
Relatives of those still missing were in tears as they prayed for their safety.
On Friday, helmeted rescuers carried a body wrapped in a white covering on a stretcher across a mound of shattered concrete and tangled steel bars. Others were trying to reach into gaps in the wreckage in a congested residential area.

item.title: A Ukraine loan is in limbo after EU budget talks stall. Leaders will try again in 3 weeks
item.description:
A Ukraine loan is in limbo after EU budget talks stall. Leaders will try again in 3 weeks
European Council President António Costa says European Union leaders have failed to agree on the 2028-2034 budgetByLORNE COOK Associated PressNovember 27, 2026, 7:23 AM
BRUSSELS -- After struggling to chaperone Europe’s leaders through more than 12 hours of high-stakes budget negotiations, European Council President António Costa faced reporters early Friday with a stark assessment. “We didn’t reach an agreement,” he said.
Government leaders from the 27-nation European Union failed to narrow down the size of the 2028-2034 budget — let alone how it might be used. An important loan for Ukraine was caught up in the wrangling.
The spending package is small compared to national budgets — around 1% to 1.2% of gross national income — but it encapsulates the ambitions of the world’s biggest trading bloc and how it sees itself on the international stage.
Costa said “some member states asked for further reductions" in how much they would have to pay in, according to his latest proposals, while most were "opposed to further cuts, and some even proposed to reverse some cuts.”
It was a day of brinksmanship that saw the leaders playing tough for national audiences.
In three weeks, they will try again. The stakes are high. Elections in some key countries are approaching, and new hardline governments or shaky coalitions could complicate matters further.
In coming days, Costa will draw his conclusions from the summit talks — held in two plenary sessions, several group meetings, and the corridor conversations that typify EU budget negotiations — and consult again with capitals.
Some leaders, notably from countries that pay more into the budget than they get back in allocations, skipped certain meetings. But Costa, a former Portuguese prime minister, was unruffled.
“This is a negotiation process,” he said. “It’s normal that the member states try to defend their own national interests.” ...

item.title: Zelenskyy urges the US to pressure Putin, calling Trump’s 'my friend' remark strange
item.description:
Zelenskyy urges the US to pressure Putin, calling Trump’s 'my friend' remark strange
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed frustration with the U.S. approach to Russian leader Vladimir PutinBySAMYA KULLAB Associated Press and ELISE MORTON Associated PressNovember 27, 2026, 6:22 AM
KYIV, Ukraine -- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expressed frustration with the U.S. stance toward Russian leader Vladimir Putin, in the latest sign of deepening tension between Kyiv and Washington just as a question mark appears over Europe’s future financial commitments to Kyiv.
Zelenskyy said in an interview with the BBC broadcast Friday that he wants the U.S. to apply more pressure on Putin to stop his invasion of Ukraine, which began almost five years ago and grinds on despite President Donald Trump’s efforts to broker a peace deal.
The Ukrainian president described Trump calling Putin “my friend” at a recent summit in China as “strange” because the Russian leader is “an aggressor and a killer.”
“He can’t be a friend,” Zelenskyy told the British broadcaster in Kyiv, likening it to someone calling Adolf Hitler a friend during World War II.
The International Criminal Court has issued an arrest warrant for Putin for war crimes, accusing him of personal responsibility for the abductions of children from Ukraine. The Trump administration, meanwhile, has imposed sweeping sanctions on the court as part of its campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the U.S. and its allies including Israel.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Zelenskyy was “insulting his counterpart,” showing that the Ukrainian leader “is not willing to follow the path of (a) peace settlement.”
Zelenskyy’s comments were broadcast a day after Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law and a U.S. envoy trying to mediate an end to the war, complimented Putin on being a “grandmaster” of politics and weeks after Kushner’s partner in peace efforts, Steve Witkoff, described Putin as ...

item.title: Houthis report 11 killed, including children, in an airstrike, and other Mideast news
item.description:
Houthis report 11 killed, including children, in an airstrike, and other Mideast news
Houthi rebels say an airstrike in southwestern Yemen has killed at least 11 people, including childrenBySUZAN FRASER Associated Press, MUNIR AHMED Associated Press, and FATMA KHALED Associated PressNovember 27, 2026, 6:17 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
The Iran-backed Houthi rebels report that an air strike in southwestern Yemen has killed at least 11 people, including children.
Meanwhile, top officials from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey are holding a meeting of their defense pact that is expected to discuss Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. And a senior Hamas official says the son of the group's leader was targeted by an Israeli strike but survived.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Friday. Read our full coverage here.
The Houthi-run health ministry said Friday that a strike on a densely populated area in southwestern Yemen killed at least 11 people, including children, the latest attack in the fight between the Iran-backed rebel group and government forces backed by Saudi Arabia.
Ministry spokesperson Anees al-Asbahi said on X that an airstrike hit a cinema building in Turbah city in Taiz province early Friday morning, killing people including children who sold ice cream in the area and had been living in part of the building. Al-Asbahi didn’t provide details of how many children were killed and said the death toll was preliminary as rescuers are trying to pull out more bodies from under the rubble.
He blamed the strike on Saudi Arabia. The AP couldn’t independently verify his claims and the Saudi coalition made no public comment about this incident.
Footage aired by Houthi-controlled al-Masirah TV showed a destroyed building and people digging through the rubble to recover the bodies of several children. The AP couldn’t independently verify the footage.
